Building Insurance Claim-Risk Prediction — A Data-Science Case Study¶

Problem. From twelve descriptors of an insured building (structure, size, location, coverage period), estimate the probability it files a claim during the insured period, and turn that probability into an underwriting triage decision.

Why it is framed this way. The two errors are not symmetric: a missed claim means under-pricing and under-reserving; a false alarm costs an analyst a few minutes. The work therefore optimises claim recall at a deliberately chosen operating point, and calibrates the scores so a probability means what it says.

Contents

  1. Data provenance & setup
  2. Exploratory analysis
  3. Features — and a leakage study that changed the headline numbers
  4. Modelling
  5. Evaluation (out-of-fold)
  6. Probability calibration
  7. Business interpretation: threshold, risk bands, triage policy
  8. Deployment & train/serve parity
  9. Conclusions and limitations

Every number is produced by src_pipeline.py / diagnostics.py, the code the API and the Streamlit app run. This notebook defines no functions of its own.

How provenance is decided. data/make_dataset.py writes a SHA-256 fingerprint whenever it generates the CSVs. 2. Exploratory analysis¶

  • Class imbalance: about 78% no-claim vs 22% claim. Predicting "no claim" everywhere scores 78% accuracy and is useless for triage, so accuracy is not the target metric.
  • Building Dimension is heavily right-skewed with outliers; median imputation plus a P99 cap keeps a few extremes from dominating the scaler.
  • Building_Type carries the clearest signal.
  • Geo_Code has ~1,100 levels for ~5,000 rows (≈4.5 buildings per zone). That ratio matters a great deal in section 3.

3. Features — and a leakage study¶

Engineered features (defined once in src_pipeline.transform):

Feature Rationale
Geo_Code_enc Smoothed claim rate of the building's zone (target encoding)
risk_score Composite of type, fencing, garden, residential, zone
dim_per_window Size per window, a construction-density proxy
is_large Above the 75th-percentile footprint
short_period Half-year coverage flag

The finding that changed the headline numbers¶

An earlier version of this project fitted the Geo target encoding on all training rows before splitting, so each validation row's encoding contained its own label. The cell below measures the effect under identical 5-fold cross-validation. On generated data there is also a hard ceiling: the generator's own noise-free formula. No honest model can beat it.

In [4]:
study = leakage_study(train_csv)
rows = [("Geo map fitted on all rows (own label leaks)", study["auc_leaky_geo_encoding"]),
        ("Fold-safe + out-of-fold Geo encoding (current)", study["auc_fold_safe"]),
        ("Fold-safe, Geo features removed", study["auc_fold_safe_without_geo"])]
if study["auc_oracle_generating_formula"] is not None:
    rows.append(("CEILING: the generator's true formula, no noise", study["auc_oracle_generating_formula"]))
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["setup", "5-fold CV AUC"]).round(4)
Out[4]:
setup 5-fold CV AUC
0 Geo map fitted on all rows (own label leaks) 0.8257
1 Fold-safe + out-of-fold Geo encoding (current) 0.6728
2 Fold-safe, Geo features removed 0.6741
3 CEILING: the generator's true formula, no noise 0.6897

Reading the table. The leaky setup scores above the theoretical ceiling, which is impossible without leakage. The whole difference was the Geo encoding memorising labels. Fitted honestly, the Geo features add nothing measurable: with ≈4.5 buildings per zone, smoothing (correctly) pulls almost every zone back to the global rate. The fold-safe pipeline lands within ~0.02 of the ceiling, so the model is extracting nearly all the signal there is.

The fix, now in src_pipeline: the target map is fitted only on training folds, and training rows receive an out-of-fold encoding, so no building's feature ever contains its own label. Geo codes are also canonicalised ('0042', 42 and 42.0 are the same zone). A float/string mismatch had previously made the deployed API ignore Geo entirely (section 8).

4. Modelling¶

train_full runs the whole protocol:

  1. stratified 80/20 split; preprocessing fitted on the 80% only; SMOTE and scaling on the training part only;
  2. eight candidates compared on the held-out 20% (logistic regression → tuned gradient-boosted trees → a soft-voting ensemble);
  3. the champion is re-evaluated out-of-fold on every training row (5 folds, with preprocessing, Geo encoding, SMOTE and scaling refit inside each fold);
  4. its scores are calibrated (section 6), the threshold is chosen, and the deployable model is refit on all rows.
In [5]:

Why logistic regression wins. With honest features the signal is weak and close to additive. That's how the generator built it, and it's a common shape in tabular insurance data too. Flexible ensembles have nothing extra to model and spend their variance fitting SMOTE's synthetic minority points. The regularised linear model generalises best and stays auditable: each coefficient is a readable risk driver.

6. Probability calibration¶

SMOTE trains the model on a 50/50 class mix, so its raw scores describe a world where half of all buildings claim. On a portfolio where about 22% do, a raw 0.50 is not a 50% risk. Risk bands and any pricing use need probabilities that match observed frequencies.

Two calibrators are fitted on the out-of-fold raw scores and evaluated cross-fitted (each fold calibrated by a map learned on the other folds): Platt scaling (a logistic curve on the raw logit, which suits the prior shift SMOTE introduces) and isotonic regression (non-parametric). The one with lower held-out log-loss, a proper scoring rule, is deployed.

In [9]:
cal = tm.metrics["calibration"]
table = pd.DataFrame(
    [("raw (SMOTE-trained)", cal["log_loss_raw"], cal["brier_raw"], cal["ece_raw"], cal["mean_pred_raw"])] +
    [(f"calibrated · {k}", v["log_loss"], v["brier"], v["ece"], oof[f"p_{k}"].mean())
     for k, v in cal["comparison"].items()],
    columns=["scores", "log-loss", "Brier", "ECE", "mean predicted"]).round(4)
print(f"Observed claim rate: {cal['base_rate']:.4f}   |   deployed calibrator: {cal['method']}")
table

bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 11)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
for col, color, name in [("p_raw", "#c0392b", "raw"), ("p_sigmoid", "#2c7fb8", "Platt"),
                         ("p_isotonic", "#27ae60", "isotonic")]:
    s = oof[col].to_numpy(); idx = np.clip(np.digitize(s, bins) - 1, 0, 9)
    pts = [(s[idx == b].mean(), y[idx == b].mean()) for b in range(10) if (idx == b).sum() >= 10]
    ax[0].plot(*zip(*pts), "o-", color=color, label=name)
ax[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="grey", label="perfect")
ax[0].set_xlabel("mean predicted (bin)"); ax[0].set_ylabel("observed claim rate (bin)")
ax[0].set_title("Reliability diagram (out-of-fold)"); ax[0].legend()
ax[1].hist(oof["p_raw"], bins=40, alpha=.55, color="#c0392b", label="raw")
ax[1].hist(oof["p_calibrated"], bins=40, alpha=.55, color="#2c7fb8", label="calibrated (deployed)")
ax[1].axvline(cal["base_rate"], color="black", ls="--", label="true base rate")
ax[1].legend(); ax[1].set_title("Score distribution")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Raw scores overstate risk by roughly 2× across the whole range. After calibration the mean predicted probability equals the observed claim rate, and the reliability curve follows the diagonal. The remaining gap is at the very top, where the few highest-scored buildings are somewhat over-predicted (see the Élevé row in section 7). Platt and isotonic perform almost the same; Platt wins narrowly and has no step artefacts in the sparse high-risk tail.

7. Business interpretation¶

7.1 Threshold as a business lever¶

The decision threshold is chosen on calibrated out-of-fold scores to maximise F1 subject to recall ≥ 70% on claims: the insurer refuses to let more than ~30% of real claims through without review. The cost of that guarantee, on a signal this weak, is reviewing a large share of the portfolio. The trade-off is stated explicitly here rather than hidden.

In [11]:
op = tm.metrics["oof_at_threshold"]
print(f"Threshold (calibrated probability): {tm.threshold:.3f}")
print(f"Recall {op['recall']:.1%} | Precision {op['precision']:.1%} | F1 {op['f1']:.3f}")
print(f"Share of portfolio flagged for review: {tm.metrics['flagged_share']:.1%}")
for t in [0.15, tm.threshold, 0.25, 0.30, 0.40]:
    flag = p >= t
    print(f"  threshold {t:.3f}: review {flag.mean():5.1%} of buildings -> catch "
          f"{y[flag].sum() / y.sum():5.1%} of claims (precision {y[flag].mean():.1%})")

7.2 Risk bands → triage policy¶

Bands are defined on the calibrated scale relative to the portfolio's own claim rate, so they keep their meaning if the data changes:

Band Calibrated probability Action
Faible below the portfolio rate Auto-approve / fast-track
Moyen 1–2× the portfolio rate Standard manual review
Élevé above 2× the portfolio rate Senior underwriter + inspection

The table below compares each band's predicted probability with the observed claim rate of the buildings in it (out-of-fold).

In [12]:
bands = pd.DataFrame(tm.metrics["bands"])
bands["edges"] = [f"< {tm.band_edges[0]:.3f}", f"{tm.band_edges[0]:.3f}–{tm.band_edges[1]:.3f}",
                  f">= {tm.band_edges[1]:.3f}"]
bands["× portfolio rate (observed)"] = bands["observed_rate"] / tm.metrics["base_rate"]
bands["action"] = bands["band"].map(TRIAGE_ACTION)
bands[["band", "edges", "n", "share", "mean_predicted", "observed_rate",
       "× portfolio rate (observed)", "action"]].round(3)
Out[12]:
band edges n share mean_predicted observed_rate × portfolio rate (observed) action
0 Faible < 0.221 2797 0.558 0.144 0.145 0.657 Auto-approve / fast-track underwriting
1 Moyen 0.221–0.442 2057 0.410 0.305 0.311 1.405 Route to standard manual review
2 Élevé >= 0.442 158 0.032 0.490 0.399 1.804 Escalate to senior underwriter + request inspe...

Observed risk rises monotonically across the bands, which is the property a triage policy needs. The Élevé band is deliberately narrow (about 3% of buildings). On this signal very few buildings can be confidently placed at twice the average risk, and its observed rate (≈1.8×) is a little below its predicted rate. A narrow escalation queue fits a scarce resource like senior underwriters, but its stated probabilities should be read as "high, likely somewhat overstated".

8. Deployment & train/serve parity¶

Here the notebook loads the deployed bundle in models/, the exact artefact the FastAPI service and the Streamlit app load, and scores the test portfolio through score_frame. It then checks two things:

  1. the model retrained in this notebook and the deployed bundle agree;
  2. this output matches predictions_test.csv written by train.py.

The result is saved to notebooks/notebook_predictions.csv; tests/test_parity.py sends the same raw rows to the running API and requires identical answers.

Why this section exists: the earlier version stored Geo codes as float keys that became strings after the JSON round-trip, so the deployed API silently ignored location and disagreed with the published predictions on 710 of 2,147 buildings. No test compared the two paths. Now one does.

In [14]:
deployed = TrainedModel.load(os.path.join(ROOT, "models"))
scored = deployed.score_frame(test)
scored.insert(0, "customer_id", test["Customer Id"].to_numpy())
scored.to_csv("notebook_predictions.csv", index=False)

in_notebook = tm.score_frame(test)
published = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(ROOT, "predictions_test.csv"))
print("max |p| difference, notebook-trained vs deployed bundle :",
      float(np.abs(in_notebook["claim_probability"] - scored["claim_probability"]).max()))
print("max |p| difference, deployed bundle vs train.py output  :",
      float(np.abs(published["claim_probability"] - scored["claim_probability"]).max()))
print("decision mismatches vs train.py output                 :",
      int((published["prediction"] != scored["prediction"]).sum()))
print("\nTest predictions:", scored["prediction"].value_counts().to_dict())
print("Risk bands      :", scored["risk_level"].value_counts().reindex(BAND_NAMES).to_dict())

Serving the model¶

python train.py                               # trains, evaluates, writes models/ + predictions
uvicorn api.main:app --reload --port 8000     # REST API -> http://localhost:8000/docs
streamlit run app/streamlit_app.py            # interactive app
pytest -q                                     # full test suite, including parity

9. Conclusions and limitations¶

What this project shows (figures quoted for the generated dataset; the live cells above recompute them for whatever data is in data/)

  • Leakage, measured and removed. Target encoding fitted before the split inflated AUC from ≈0.67 to ≈0.83, above the generator's theoretical ceiling. The fold-safe pipeline sits within ~0.02 of that ceiling.
  • Calibrated probabilities. SMOTE-trained scores overstated risk about 2×. Cross-fitted Platt scaling brings the mean prediction to the observed rate and cuts expected calibration error from ≈0.25 to <0.01.
  • A decision, not a metric. An explicit recall guarantee, bands tied to the portfolio claim rate with their observed rates reported, and a stated review-cost trade-off.
  • Train/serve parity under test. Notebook, train.py, API and app share one scoring method, and the test suite checks that they agree.

Limitations, stated plainly

  • Unless data_source above reads real, every number describes a generated dataset that mimics the competition schema. The method transfers; the magnitudes do not.
  • The signal is weak (AUC ≈0.67). Holding 70% recall means reviewing about 60% of the portfolio, and the top band is slightly over-predicted.
  • Geo_Code adds nothing at ≈4.5 buildings per zone. A hierarchical encoding (zone → region) or external geographic data would be the next lever.
  • Thresholds optimise F1 under a recall constraint. With claim severity data they should minimise expected monetary loss instead.
